about: Every message Aaron typed or dictated in this session on Terra (the PC), copied verbatim from its log on 25 September 2026. Only his words. Taken from both places the log keeps them - the queued record of every message he sends and the plain user records - each message kept once at its earliest time. Messages he sent while Claude was still working sit in time order with the rest and are not marked apart, because a queued record alone does not show that. System text, tool output, skill instructions, task notifications, cross-session messages, compaction summaries and anything the studio wrote are excluded, as are the helper agents' logs beside this one.
title: Manifest Disunity Game Design Document

messages.text:
# Role

You are acting as the Game Designer on Manifest Disunity.

You are not a programmer and not a technical designer. Your job is
organization, articulation, and translation — not invention. You take
design work that already exists, much of it scattered or implicit, and
assemble it into a professional Game Design Document that the next
person downstream can actually work from.

Two rules govern everything you do here:

1. **Do not invent mechanics.** If the design work doesn't specify
   something, that's a gap. Name it as a gap. Don't fill it with a
   plausible-sounding answer — a design doc that quietly invents is worse
   than one with holes in it, because the holes are at least visible.
2. **Do not resolve open design questions.** Where something is
   ambiguous, contested, or explicitly undecided, surface it as an open
   question for me to decide. That call is mine, not yours.

# Context: where this sits in the process

Our phase order is now:

**Game Design (GDD) → Technical Design (TDD) → Production / build order
→ Implementation.**

This GDD is the deliverable that closes out the design phase. Its
specific downstream reader is a **Technical Designer**, who will take it
one system at a time and write a Technical Design Document: actual
formulas, pseudocode, inputs/outputs, and edge cases.

That reader is who you are organizing for. Every structural decision you
make — how you split the docs, what order sections go in, what each doc
declares about its dependencies — should be made to serve a TDD pass
that works system-by-system without having to re-read everything each
time.

# Source material

Read everything in `docs/design/` and the root `DESIGN.md`.

`DESIGN.md` is unusually precise for a design doc — it already contains
real formulas, named tunables, and measured numbers. **Preserve that
precision.** Where it states something exactly, carry it forward exactly.
Do not summarize a formula into prose. Do not round a measured number or
drop the measurement that justifies it. The precision is the value.

If you find design decisions referenced but never fully specified
anywhere in the repo, collect them rather than resolving them (see
"Gaps" below).

# Step 1: Orient before you propose

Before proposing any structure, read the source material and report back
to me:

- What systems you found, and which ones are specified deeply versus
  thinly.
- Which of the master-doc sections below are **already answered**
  somewhere in the source material, which are **partially** answered, and
  which are **absent entirely**. Be honest about the absent ones — I
  expect several, particularly on the pitch layer.
- Any place where two documents appear to disagree with each other.

# Step 2: Propose the split, then stop

Propose the full document structure:

- Every file you intend to create (master + each satellite), with its
  path.
- A one-line purpose for each.
- Its "Depends on" list.

Then **stop and wait for my approval.** Do not write content into any
file until I've said go.

For the satellite split: use your own judgment as a designer about where
the real seams in this design are. `DESIGN.md`'s existing section breaks
are a starting point, not an answer — if a different split serves a TDD
pass better, propose that instead and tell me why. Systems that are
tightly coupled may belong together; a section that's doing two jobs may
belong apart.

# The master document

Short. This is the tip of the iceberg — high-level orientation plus
pointers to where the depth lives. If it starts restating what's in a
satellite, it's too long.

Sections (from the pitch template we're working from):

- **Working title**
- **Concept statement** — the game in one or two sentences.
- **Target audience** — who this is actually for. "Everyone" is not an
  answer.
- **Player experience and POV** — who the player is, the setting, the
  fantasy the game grants, the emotions it's going for, the major phases
  of a playthrough.
- **Unique Selling Points** — three or four. What makes this different
  from every other grand strategy game. This has to answer "why would
  someone stop playing Paradox games and play this instead."
- **Genre(s)**
- **Visual / audio style**
- **Platform(s) and primary technology**
- **Schedule and scope** — including what is deliberately out of scope.
- **Game world fiction** — the world as presented to the player, in
  player-facing terms.
- **Core loops** — how the player's actions and the game's systems form
  loops, and why those loops are engaging. This is the "one more turn"
  question: what pulls a player into the next turn, moment to moment.
  Note the staggered timers already in the design (election schedules,
  movement growth toward ceilings, pressure clocks, rate-limited power
  stocks, cooldowns) and how they do or don't surface to the player.
- **Objectives and progression** — short-term and long-term goals,
  explicit and implicit, from first turn to endgame.
- **Game systems** — the system map: what exists, which are internal
  simulation and which the player directly interacts with, and how they
  connect. This is the index into the satellites.
- **Interactivity** — what kind of engagement each player action asks
  for (perceptual, short-term cognitive, long-term cognitive, emotional,
  social, cultural), and what the player is actually doing moment to
  moment.

Also in the master document, because multiple satellites depend on them
and nobody should have to guess which satellite owns a shared concept:

- **Cross-cutting concepts** — the two-axis ideology model and the
  affinity function, the Why record shape, the columnar state model, the
  phase-ordering discipline, the plan/resolve contract, and anything else
  you find that several systems rely on.

Several of these sections — particularly concept statement, USPs, target
audience, genre, player experience, and core loops — are likely **absent
or only implicit** in the source material, which is systems-deep and
pitch-thin. Draft them from what the design actually is, mark each one
clearly as a **draft for my review**, and don't present them as settled.

# The satellite documents

One per system. Each contains:

1. **Depends on** — a line at the top naming every other satellite (or
   the master doc) whose concepts, state, or formulas this system relies
   on. This is what lets someone working on one system know exactly what
   else to pull in, and nothing more than that.
2. **The system itself** — its mechanics, in whatever order best serves
   someone about to turn it into formulas and pseudocode. Foundational
   state and shared math legible first; dependent behavior after.
   Carry forward every existing formula, tunable name, and measured
   number for this system.
3. **Open questions** — seeded with everything already flagged as
   undecided or untested for this system (`DESIGN.md` §12 is an obvious
   source, but look everywhere). It is fine if this section is short or
   empty for some systems. It exists so that playtest findings have a
   home to be filed into directly later, without a second pass through
   every document.
4. **Gaps** — anything referenced but never specified. Separate from
   open questions: an open question is a decision I haven't made, a gap
   is something that may already have been decided and simply isn't
   written down anywhere.

# Style

- Write for a smart reader who hasn't seen this project before, but
  don't pad. No filler, no restating a section's title as its first
  sentence.
- Prefer precision over polish. A formula stated exactly beats a
  paragraph describing it well.
- Where the source material gives a reason for a decision, keep the
  reason. "Why it is this way" is the single most useful thing in a
  design doc and the first thing lost in a rewrite.

# Now begin

Start with Step 1. Report what you found, then propose the split, then
wait for me.

messages.text: Can we work on figure out the turn design before you do the rest of this? Like the ideation part and what you need for the GDD

I think we need to ignore everything about how turn design is built in the current game and we need to come up with a brand new idea as if that had never been a thing.

The two games that I draw a lot of inspiration for this is EU4 and Civ2.


Civ2 has great turn design structure so much so that "just one more turn" has become a meme. I feel like Civ2 is great because units all have different movement speeds and terrain impacts that, settlers and engineers take different times to do certain actions, and with multiple cities and units there are multiple things going on at one time.

EU4 seems to take that idea and really amplify that. Because there are the mission goals you are working towards, then there are the smaller goals you are working towards working towards those, then when you have peace treaty you can still be doing things to improve your country with diplomacy, drilling armies, etc. 

So I think the thing I learn from them is that a turn needs to have multiple things that you can do, but they should never be something that you can acomplish in one turn (in theory) and the kind of things that can be done in one turn should just be like eu4 where a pop window shows up and you just click on something and it resolves it.

The other thing to think about is that the choice the user makes is basically three parts:

* reactive - something happens and they have to decide what to do, which should have the option to ignore it which will have a consequence to it. I did have an idea of using the cliche of a newspaper pop up window with some news of things happening and what the effects are and what your options are to fix it.
* proactive - something that the player does to advance her goals in the game. 
* development of your country - something you can do to make your country stronger which may or may not interact with your goals explicitly. 


One thing I like about EU4 that they do in order to balance user actions (which isn't a perfect parallel since it is real time not turn based) is the use of admin/diplo/military points to do actions and these actions are either:

1. Research (which is necessary to progress in the game at all and the main way to use points)
2. Reactive/fixing problems (boosting stability, losing diplo points for having too many relations, using military points to boost your legitamacy)
3. Proactive (changing culture, improving cities, etc)
4. Random events that pop up and make you consider is 50 admin points worth loosing the 300 duccats


So I like that EU4 is a real time game but still constrains you in each of these areas and it is one of those things you could have a really high military research level and crush your opponents and make a lot of money that way but you could also be so adfvanced in military that you are missing out on trade increases. So like all the systems work together to both make the other more powerful but also work in the opposite way. 

I feel like with military you should have one reaction and one action phase. Someone invades you need to send troops to the border (reactive) and active (make a counter assalut on their southern counties. 

With trade I feel like there should be an unlimited ammount of trades you can make but they take another turn to be approved? 

Then diplomacy and other things I am not sure. 

I think the other thing that is missing in general is the actual goals of the game. That is what make EU4 so much fun - is the guided play of the goals that every time you play things are different. When you are playing as France sometimes the HRE is a huge pain in the ass but other times Spain allies England and you've got to fight them off first. 

So I think along with turn design we need to make sure that the GDD has three missions to be built into the alpha that would interact with the different ways of playing the game.

My thoughts are that we would want one of them to be a texas nation (and they would all have the same mission tree), Deseret (because they are a sepratist movement already realized and because I live in Utah I can write a lot about that from a story perspective), and a great lakes nation like wisconsin or minnesota beacuse that could either be the farmers union/federation mechanic. 

Those are all of my thoughts - what do you think and what can we take from these to implement into turn and game mission/goals?
I am going to say yes, but it is going to be very small and limited.

One possible thing that I like is this idea of progress bars or clocks. Like you want to influence the sepratists movement in the state over - well it is going to cost 5 million dollars over 2 years so that cost would be broken up over that time and you can see where things are and the progress of it. 

And you in theory could spend more money to speed things up but with every action there is also a opposite reaction. 

Spend a lot of money trying to arm a sepratist movement in another state - well greater chance the other country finds out.

So you pick all the things you want to do and it starts working on them and then you hit end turn and you get a news briefing (either a newspaper article like screen where you click on different things to see the status you want, or it is more like a presidential briefing of the status of everything, what countries said in response to what you asked (trade, diplomatic deals, etc)

And agree with that reading

There should be three sections the two you mentioned and a third one, but smaller about world affairs. This will be important because I want this to be where worldwide effects (like panama canal shuts down - trade impact to every nation is x% of something - this is just an example). The world wide section would also be a good area to build out the world diegetically.
The world markets will change yes but small.

The thing I like about the EU4 mission tree setup is:

1. It gives you direction to play
2. It gives you challenges to the play
3. It gives the play a story
4. It gives you bonuses if you accomplished them in order to keep the momentum up.


With that in mind here are some of the rough ideas for the Texas Missions:

1. Become accepted on the world stage
   1. Have one nation larger than you accept you as a soverign nation (once completed this gives you a small bonus to your trade)
   2. Have over 50% of the nation recognize you as a soverign nation (once completed this gives you a bonus to your authority or influence or something - as an example)
   3. Receive 100% nations (excluding other texas nations) recognize you (and in the game it would mean that if all countries accept you then you would be accepted worldwide so you would get a bonus from world trades)

   4. Own and control Dallas (gets the Well, that's Dallas bonus - increased recognition of soverignty from nations west of the mississippi. 
   5. Own and control Austin (gets the Father of Texas bonus - texas counties you conquer don't have as much civil unrest and it lowers quicker, increased likelyhood of taking over counties from other texas counties, maybe something more - the idea being this would be the most powerful bonus because it gives austin a better fighting chance).
   6. Those all would be done in any order but once all are conquered
      1. Own and control every county in texas (get texas united - lowers civil unrest)
      2. Former Glory, control all of the counties that were apart of the republic of texas (get a bonus of authority maybe?
      3. Choke the farmers, control the mississippi choke point and all mississippi river counties in the south area (get a bonus on trade or something?)
      4. Dominate the Gulf, control at least 50% of the ports along the gulf of mexico (get a bonus where you can charge nations 10% more on trade and they will still accept / or the other way around) 
      5. We never wanted to be apart of your country anyways (the name of it maybe), conquer Washington D.C. (gain the ability to unite the entire map as the united states of Texas (instead of the USA). So this would change your objective and make you fight against Philidalphia and NYC. 
3. Country Development
   1. Texas BBQ - have 110% of food needs for 2 years (some bonus with quality of life for a certain time?)
   2. Texas Oil - resource goal? 
   3. And I don't know maybe other ones for the other things? 


These are just my ideas brainstorming
